catalog_quote: The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High (H = ') and Low (L = v), which may combine on a given syllable (with restricted and varying distribution) to give Falling (H+L = "), and less frequently, Rising (L+H = ") tones. ... In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H, which has the effect of lowering the 'ceiling' for subsequent H tone realization. Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. [p.47] ... Unfortunately, Ward's discussion of stress does not go any deeper than suggesting stress is related to verb stems, and in fact, it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward32. [p.55] [fn.32] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. Faraclas (1984b) presents an analysis of Obolo incorporating phrasal stress. [fn.34, p.56] ... as the foot is a notion usually associated with stress phenomena, it is by no means clear how it would apply in a non-stress language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: All Lower Cross languages (Okobo explicitly included in the study, data first-hand) are two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone languages with contrastive downstep; the author finds no real evidence for word stress (rejecting Ward's 1933 verb-root stress for Efik) and treats LC as 'non-stress' languages, allowing only probable phrasal stress and stress-marking of compound-word junctures. No syllable position is named as stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Possible phrasal stress and stress at junctures of compound words (fn.32); Faraclas (1984b) analyses Obolo with phrasal stress; Connell 1994 p.12 adds that tone interacts with phrasal stress but 'no investigation in this area has been done' beyond Obolo.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement for Lower Cross as a whole, argued mainly from Efik/Ibibio material; Okobo is not named in the stress passage (it is named in the tone, consonant and vowel-length sections). Word-level stress denied; phrase-level stress conjectured, uninvestigated.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statements are group-level claims about all Lower Cross languages in Connell's 19-language study (Okobo, okob1241, explicitly included with first-hand 1988 field data, '50,000 speakers (two dialects)', Okobo LGA, Akwa Ibom); the stress discussion itself is argued from Efik (efik1245) and generalised to 'Efik or the other LC languages'. No Okobo-specific prosodic description exists.

sources.note: Okobo in the sample (p.4, p.6, p.7, p.9 no length contrast). Sec. 3.3 p.10: 'in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep (D).. Sec. 5 p.12: 'Tonal systems in the group appear to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress statement.
